summary: Defines requirements for emulating Time Division Multiplexed circuits, including PDH and SONET/SDH, across packet-switched networks. It is aligned with the Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge architecture. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Old phone lines carry data in fixed time slots. This memo lists what is needed to make a modern packet network imitate those old lines.

questions: tdm circuit emulation over packet networks
how do packet networks carry t1 and e1 circuits
subtitle: What a packet network must do to imitate the fixed-rate telephone circuits (T1, E1, SONET/SDH) that carry TDM traffic.

tldr.problem: Telephone-style circuits (TDM) send bits at a fixed rate with tightly controlled timing, and the generic pseudo wire requirements do not cover those specifics.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists requirements for carrying PDH and SONET/SDH circuits across a packet-switched network as pseudo wires, covering clock handling, packet loss, ordering, signaling, bandwidth, delay variation, congestion and fault detection.
tldr.outcome: It specifies requirements only, not a protocol. It complements the general pseudo wire requirements in RFC 3916 and is an Informational memo.

today: RFC 4197 is an Informational RFC (October 2005) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sets out requirements and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why TDM Needs Its Own Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 4197 defines the requirements for edge-to-edge emulation of circuits that carry Time Division Multiplexed (TDM) signals over a packet-switched network (PSN). It covers the Plesiochronous Digital Hierarchy (PDH) and SONET/SDH, and it follows the Pseudo Wire Emulation Edge-to-Edge (PWE3) architecture from RFC 3985.

The generic pseudo wire requirements in RFC 3916 do not cover what is special about TDM. The motivation section names several things: the clocks at the two ends must stay in balance, and the jitter and wander of the output clock must stay within limits despite packet delay variation. Voice traffic wants minimal one-way delay and tolerates some data errors, while signaling traffic tolerates delay but is sensitive to errors. Customers also expect problems in the packet network to be isolated from problems beyond it, and they are sensitive to misconnection and unexpected connection termination.
sections.eli5: Old phone circuits are fussy about timing. This memo adds the extra rules a packet network must follow to keep those circuits happy.

sections.title: TDM Circuits and Transport Modes
sections.content:
TDM bit rates differ by region. The memo gives the T1 stream of 1.544 Mbps and the T3 stream of 44.736 Mbps for North America, and the E1 stream of 2.048 Mbps and the E3 stream of 34.368 Mbps for Europe. Bit rates are multiples of 8000, so a T1 frame is 193 bits and an E1 frame is 256 bits.

The RFC separates unstructured TDM (a raw bit stream with every bit available as payload) from structured TDM (with frames, channels called timeslots, or multiframes). That leads to two transport modes:

  • Structure-agnostic transport carries the bits as they are, with any structural overhead passed along transparently.
  • Structure-aware transport takes some of the structure into account, so synchronization bits may be stripped at the ingress and regenerated at the egress.

For channel signaling, the memo describes CAS (Channel-Associated Signaling, carried in the same frame and cycling through multiframes of 12, 16 or 24 frames) and CCS (Common Channel Signaling, a separate channel, typically HDLC-based, such as SS7 or ISDN PRI signaling). SONET/SDH circuits carry substantial transport overhead for monitoring and fault isolation, and the memo covers emulation of STS-1 SPE, concatenated STS-Nc payloads and sub-STS-1 Virtual Tributaries.
sections.eli5: A TDM circuit is like a conveyor belt with numbered slots. You can ship the whole belt as one lump, or you can look at the slots and handle them one by one.

sections.title: Reference Model and Clock Scenarios
sections.content:
The generic PWE3 models in RFC 3985 apply without change. All services in the memo are special cases of the Bit-stream and Structured bit-stream payload types. The new piece is a network synchronization model that labels the clocks (A to L) at the customer edge (CE) devices, the provider edge (PE) devices and the network. A basic requirement is that the clock a PE recovers from the incoming circuit and the clock the far PE uses to transmit it have the same frequency.

Which method fits depends on how the network is synchronized. The memo describes four scenarios, summarized in the table below. In the relative scenario, timing information MUST be explicitly transferred from the ingress PE to the egress PE. In the adaptive scenario, it MAY be, for example by RTP, and the tolerance between the two clocks must be small enough that the jitter buffer neither overflows nor underflows.
sections.eli5: Both ends of a call need to tick at the same speed. Sometimes a shared clock tells everyone the time. When there is none, one end has to guess the other end's speed from how the packets arrive.

sections.title: Emulated Services and Generic Requirements
sections.content:
Structure-agnostic transport is considered for E1, T1 (DS1), E3 and T3 (DS3). Structure-aware transport is considered for E1/T1 with framing, NxDS0 with or without CAS, SONET STS-1 SPE and SDH VC-3, STS-Nc, VT-N and their SDH analogs. There is no requirement for structure-agnostic transport of SONET/SDH.

The encapsulation and payload layers MUST conform to the common requirements of RFC 3916, with TDM-specific notes: structure-aware transport MUST get its header information from the encapsulation layer, and SONET/SDH path overhead MUST be preserved. Each sub-circuit of a multiplexed circuit MUST get separate treatment. The encapsulation layer MUST provide sequencing and SHOULD provide timing information when needed. Support for variable length PDUs is not applicable to TDM emulation.

Service-specific requirements include connectivity between attachment circuits of the same type, and network synchronization sufficient to match the ingress and egress clocks and keep egress jitter and wander within the limits in the normative references.
sections.eli5: The memo lists which kinds of old lines must be copied and says the copy must keep their pieces separate and in the right order.

sections.title: Loss, Delay, Bandwidth and Faults
sections.content:
Packet loss. Emulation MAY assume a very low probability of loss and needs no retransmission. The encapsulation layer SHOULD let the egress PE interpret each packet independently, make lost packets reliably detectable, limit the effect of loss on clock recovery and let the egress substitute data. Ordering. The encapsulation layer MUST guarantee ordered delivery: out-of-order packets MUST be detected, SHOULD be reordered if not too late or too early, and are otherwise treated as lost.

Bandwidth and delay. Larger packet payloads use the network more efficiently, while smaller payloads lower latency. The extra delay of the compensation (jitter) buffer SHOULD NOT exceed the packet delay variation seen in the network. The encapsulation layer MAY save bandwidth by not sending corrupted data or inactive channels.

Congestion. TDM circuits run at a constant rate, so the TCP-style rate adjustment does not apply, but the ability to shut down a TDM pseudo wire on congestion MUST be provided. Precautions should avoid shutting down or re-establishing many pseudo wires at once.

Faults and monitoring. The encapsulation layer SHOULD detect, handle and report misconnection or stray packets, packet loss and malformed packets, and SHOULD provide performance monitoring data compatible with classic TDM carriers. The memo also asks for compatibility with existing network infrastructure, including header compression.
sections.eli5: A phone call cannot wait for a lost word to be sent again. So the network must notice gaps, keep things in order, and not hold packets so long that the voice lags.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 3916 apply fully to TDM emulation. The memo adds one point: TDM services are sensitive to packet delay variation, so they need protection from attacks that exploit it.
sections.eli5: Because these lines need steady timing, someone who makes packets arrive unevenly can spoil the call, so that must be guarded against.
